problem: Language-guided robot navigation methods usually depend on large corpora or labeled datasets that are costly to build, which limits their use for service robots in known environments.
motivation: Service robots need natural-language interaction instead of buttons or controllers. Navigation instructions are mostly determined by landmarks and temporal words, so a lightweight, data-free pipeline built on these may be enough for a known environment.
key_idea: Build a landmark retrieval table from the known environment, use it to extract landmarks and temporal words from the instruction, sort them by weight, and publish them as sequential navigation goals.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablation evidence can be cited. The abstract implies that exploiting the known map's landmarks and temporal ordering can replace large labeled corpora.
method: Landmark extraction: extract the landmarks of the known environment and build a retrieval table of them.
Instruction landmark extraction: use the retrieval table to pull landmarks out of the natural language instruction.
Temporal word extraction: extract temporal words from the instruction.
Weight-based sorting: sort temporal words and their corresponding landmarks by their weights to get the visiting order.
Goal publishing: publish the sorted landmarks one by one as navigation goals to guide the robot.

setting.backbone: not specified in the abstract (retrieval table plus rule-based language processing)
setting.training_data: none stated; the abstract says it avoids large labeled corpora
setting.action_space: navigation goals published one by one (goal-based navigation)

results: The abstract only states that the method can guide robot navigation with natural language instructions in a known environment. It gives no quantitative results or baselines.
limitations: Limited to known environments, since the landmark retrieval table must be built in advance.
Relies on landmarks and temporal words, so it may not handle richer or more ambiguous instructions.
No quantitative evaluation or benchmark comparison is stated in the abstract.
